title: Neocloud Prime Intellect Acquires Startup To Speed Up Inference
summary: Neoclouds and so-called inference providers that help app developers run open source models are trying to differentiate themselves in a very crowded market. For instance, one such neocloud, Prime Intellect , which was valued at $1 billion in an equity financing in July, is buying a startup to help it make open models run faster and more cheaply on its Nvidia servers, compared to its rivals. Prime Intellect, based in San Francisco, is acquiring Moondream , a young developer of open-source models that has fewer than 10 employees, according to Prime Intellect co-founder and CEO Vincent Weisser . (Weisser wouldn’t share the terms of the deal, but Moondream has raised $4.5 million in funding.) San Francisco- and Seattle-based Moondream is best known for an open-source vision-language model for analyzing and understanding images, like identifying boxes in an image of a warehouse or ads in a livestream. But Prime Intellect is largely acquiring the startup for its employees’ skills in writing software to make models run more efficiently, Weisser said.

title: OpenAI Scrambles to Fix Safety Issues Before Shipping Its Next Flagship Model
summary: OpenAI is grappling with fallout from its use of a controversial innovation in AI design as it works to get its next unreleased model to a place where leaders believe they can safely release it. The model design, known as loop transformers or recurrent depth, can make it harder to monitor the way the AI “thinks,” or how it reasons and processes its response to a question or task, The Information reported last month . That means the technique could erode a key tool that OpenAI and other companies rely on to catch misbehaving models. OpenAI hasn’t publicly acknowledged the technique, but Microsoft last week accidentally confirmed OpenAI’s use of it in one of the AI company’s most advanced commercially available models, GPT-6.1 Sol, in a blog post it has since edited to remove the disclosure.

title: Rebuilding Companies for the Agentic Era
summary: Companies have spent the past few years figuring out how to put AI to work. In 2026, some are confronting a bigger question: What should a company look like when AI can understand context, coordinate work and act across systems? The Information ’s Co-Executive Editor Amir Efrati sat down with leaders from three companies at the forefront of this shift to discuss how agentic AI is changing how companies work and operate. Owen Jennings, Business Lead & Executive Officer, Block Stephanie Cohen, Chief Strategy Officer, Cloudflare Surabhi Gupta, CTO, Klaviyo Redesigning the operating model Block and Cloudflare offered two ways to rethink the operating model. For Cloudflare, Stephanie Cohen said the company had to rethink the work itself, not simply add AI tools onto existing processes. “If we didn’t redesign how work was done, we weren’t going to actually change what went on at Cloudflare,” she said. “The only way for us to redesign the factory floor was to get rid of whole functions.” At Block, the answer was to rebuild its functional model so engineering, product, design and sales teams work across Square, Cash App and Afterpay on shared capabilities. Owen Jennings said the change came about when AI agents became capable of writing production code in complex systems, prompting the company to ask how work should move when agents can share company context with humans. “We said, based on where the tools are now and based on where we think it’s going, what functions do we need at the company? How do we want to organize?” recalled Jennings. The shift is showing up in customer experiences, with Square and Cash App surfacing tools, insights or actions at the right moment, rather than relying on static, one-size-fits-all surfaces. Block shipped about three times as many Square features in the first half of 2026 as a year earlier, he said. “There’s a lot of conversation around automating things for the sake of it,” said Jennings. “For us, it’s about building useful stuff for customers.” Humans still matter Companies leaning hardest into agents aren’t necessarily trying to replace humans. Cloudflare hired 1,111 interns this year, including AI-native talent who Cohen said worked on “everything,” including old-fashioned automation no one had made time to build. “By teaching them the company and allowing them to have access to our system, they’ve shown us a million ways that what we were doing didn’t make sense,” she said. Block has also built a workspace for working alongside agents. Buzz, an open source tool the company has released for people and AI agents, gives each agent its own identity, permissions and context. “The idea is not to remove people from the loop, but to make agent work visible and steerable so humans can focus on judgment, taste and customer understanding,” Jennings said. Klaviyo wants engineers closer to customer outcomes rather than assigned tickets. “One of the things we’ve found very effective is having the engineers sit side-by-side with the partner functions, and have them become domain experts,” said Klaviyo’s Surabhi Gupta. Cloudflare runs hands-on workshops that are deliberately low-pressure, and names an AI “champion” on each team, typically someone already experimenting. “It’s easier to ask a peer than to ask someone else who you feel like is not gonna understand why you don’t know how to do everything,” Cohen said. Companies also need infrastructure connecting agents to systems, data and context. Cohen described Cloudflare’s approach as a “harness”: a layer connecting AI models with security, systems of record, company context and employee identities, while letting the company switch models as needed. “Part of the problem is people started with the hammer and were like, ‘here’s this hammer, build this house.’ The reality is you have to design the house,” said Cohen. The new metrics Agentic AI is also creating new metrics to measure success. At Block, development velocity—the pace that new features are shipped—has become a key metric. Gupta says Klaviyo measures this too, as well as cost and hours saved as a result of agents. One metric no one on the panel could predict: headcount, though Cohen felt optimistic about growth. “My guess is we’ll have more employees [in five years],” she said. “The human world is human-shaped, and humans want to interact with more humans.”

title: Why Companies Can't Prove Their AI Spending Pays Off
summary: The trillion-dollar question of the AI boom is whether businesses’ spending on the technology pays off. But measuring that return is often uncertain, confusing or incomplete. That’s because it takes time for AI to show a return on investment that can be demonstrated in a company’s income statement, as we’ve written . A new study from the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School and GBK Collective, a consultancy, echoes this idea, showing that most companies are still tracking ROI by measuring whether it makes their workers more efficient rather than whether it is driving more revenue. The study, based on online surveys of 1,400 U.S.-based employees from firms that have at least 1,000 staff and generate more than $50 million annually, showed that 40% of managers measured AI’s impact on their business in terms of “hours saved per employee” and 37% tracked how AI reduced their workers’ errors. Only about 27% of managers said they track the revenue they generate from AI features, apps and tools they provide to their customers. Perhaps worryingly, 44% of managers said that over the next one to two years, AI’s primary role will be to improve productivity and just 8% said it would be to drive new revenue or create new products.

title: Applied And Lam Are Overlooked Chip Equipment Stocks
summary: The AI chip sector has been picked clean of bargains, as stocks of chip designers, chip manufacturers and chip manufacturing equipment makers have all soared in the past year. But that doesn’t mean there aren’t still some opportunities if you know where to look. One example: Applied Materials, which makes machinery used in chip etching and deposition for memory chips—among the most highly sought-after components used in AI chips. As memory chip makers have quickly expanded manufacturing, companies like Applied and its nearest rival, Lam Research, have enjoyed surging demand for their products.
